text: Once Meridian's rogue account, scheduled task, and registry entry are gone and the gateway is patched, the billing database server still has to come back. The instinct is to grab last night's backup — but most recent and safe to restore are two different questions, and treating them as the same one is a common, costly mistake in real recovery work.

This is where Chapter 3's timeline work pays off directly. Meridian's SOC traced the earliest confirmed compromise to 11:40 PM Tuesday. The nightly backup at 1:00 AM Wednesday was captured after that — it can carry the attacker's changes baked right in. The 1:00 AM Tuesday backup, 24 hours earlier, predates the compromise and becomes the real candidate.

Predating the compromise narrows the field, but it doesn't finish the job on its own. The team restores that backup to an isolated, non-production environment first, scans it with current threat intelligence, and checks its checksum against what the backup system recorded at capture time — confirming nothing altered it after the fact.

A backup can still fail even after passing the timestamp test. It might predate this confirmed compromise but still miss an earlier, undetected stage of the same intrusion. It could have been tampered with after it was captured. Or the backup service account that created it might have been compromised independently of when the backup itself was taken.

Backup software typically runs under a broadly privileged account that can read every server it protects — exactly the kind of account worth checking against the incident's own list of confirmed-compromised credentials. A backup with an old, trustworthy-looking date is not actually known-good if the account that captured it was one the attacker also controlled.

A known-good backup has to clear both bars: it predates the confirmed compromise timestamp, and it passes scanning and integrity verification. Skip either check and the restore can quietly reintroduce exactly what eradication just removed. Next: the validation steps a system has to pass before it's trusted back in production.
